newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK stocks rebound despite budget rate fears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK stocks rebound despite budget rate fears.

text.p: The British stock market rebounded from early losses on Thursday, despite prospects of a sharp further rise in interest rates which kept the pound sterling firm and depressed the price of government bonds.
Traders said tough action on interest rates might look bad for securities prices in the short-term but the longer-term impact on both the economy and markets would be beneficial.

The FTSE 100 index of top British shares gyrated wildly as the market tried to find its feet after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget, unveiled on Wednesday. It plunged at the opening and then jumped to near record highs.

Economists said the budget was not tough enough to rein in strong consumer demand and predicted that the newly-independent Bank of England might push up interest rates by as much as 1/2 percentage point as early as next week.
Some saw official interest rates peaking at eight percent in the current cycle from 6.5 percent now.
The FTSE opened 58.5 points lower at 4,692.9 but then staged a 100-point turnaround, jumping to a peak of 4,795.2, just a whisker below its all time record of 4,796.
By mid-morning it was hovering around 4,780, a rise of 0.6 percent from the previous close.

"The average fund manager is not as gloomy as the average economist. The market is looking at the long term positive of higher interest rates rather than the short term negative," said Darren Winder, UK economist at SBC Warburg.

On the government bond market, gilts opened sharply lower, down 27/32 at 113-30/32 for the key September contract. But they crept slightly higher after a key indicator of activity in the British services sector showed a downturn in May.
Activity in the services industry has been one reflection of the strong consumer demand the Bank of England wants to tone down.
Sterling, down a little from five year highs hit immediately after the budget speech, remained firm at 2.9374/84 in mid-morning trade. It had hit a 61-month peak of 2.9430 on Wednesday.
Speaking on BBC radio on Thursday morning, Brown said his budget represented a "considerable fiscal tightening" which had helped to bring a better balance between monetary and fiscal policy.
But analysts were not convinced that any pressure had been taken off the Bank of England to raise interest rates.

"The budget...leaves the task of slowing the consumer boom to the Bank of England, meaning that interest rates are likely to rise by around 100bp (basis points) over the remainder of this year," said Paribas strategists Paul Mortimer-Lee and Nick Parsons.
Official British interest rates are now standing at 6.5 percent.
One of the main planks of Brown's budget was a windfall tax on privatised utilities, a move which had been widely flagged by the Labour government which took office two months ago.
But the "victims" of the new tax generally shrugged off its impact, with the feeling on the market that they had not been hit as hard as expected before the budget.
Airport authority BAA was up 11 pence at 583-1/2 pence and Railtrack RTK L Railtrack soared 37p to 669.
Shares in British Telecommunications Plc BT.L) leapt seven percent to a new record of 490 pence, before easing back to just under 480 pence, a rise of 21-1/2 pence.
"They seem to have got off lightly" said one trader. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
